blocks.text: Witness statement of DR ANDREW HENTON (read)
This is a statement dated 22 April 2020 from Dr Henton, who -- some of you may recall his name appears as one of the doctors in the sequence of events chart in this case. Dr Henton says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My involvement with [Baby N]’s care was quite limited and while I remember his name, I have no recollection of the case. I have had the opportunity to review his clinical notes to assist with the preparation of this statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My primary involvement seems to have been a routine review on 14 June 2016, documenting on the consultant ward round on 15 June 2016, and finally writing some blood results in the notes later that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At this time I was working for the paediatric department as a year 1 GP trainee doctor on a four-month placement working at the level of SHO.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] was born by a planned elective caesarean section on 2 June 2016 at 34 plus 4 weeks due to intrauterine growth restriction and was at high risk of having a blood clotting disorder due to his family history. A clotting disorder was confirmed following his birth.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Following stabilisation after some initial minor breathing difficulties he stabilised well on the NNU and was progressing well, with discharge planning well underway before significant deterioration with breathing problems in the early hours of 15 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Intubation failed with repeated attempts, both overnight and later in the day, following a further significant deterioration. Ultimately, the NWTS team became involved."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That being the transport team that we heard described by Dr Potter only yesterday:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] was successfully intubated and was transferred to Alder Hey Hospital later that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On Tuesday, 14 June 2016 I undertook a formalised weekly NNU review. [Baby N] had been stable in the preceding days and discharge planning was in process by this point. He was noted to be mildly jaundiced and was still on phototherapy for this. The plan was to repeat his bilirubin levels (SBR) to see if he needed to continue phototherapy. He was also to have a corrected calcium level checked as this was noted as elevated at 3.1 at 01.40 hours that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I documented a discussion with his mother of the plan, which was very much with the intention to get him home later that week. Medication for his discharge had been requested and a follow-up with Dr Caswell, a haematologist at Alder Hey, was to be arranged.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 10 am, Wednesday, 15 June 2016, I documented in the notes during a ward round with the paediatric consultant Dr Saladi."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: For reference, if anyone wants to know, that's tile 167:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "A summary of events overnight is noted where [Baby N] had desaturated and intubation had been attempted three times but was unsuccessful. At this stage [Baby N] was on BiPAP, has intravenous fluids and has received intravenous antibiotics in case of sepsis. At this stage, due to some blood noted in the oropharynx overnight, Alder Hey haematology have already advised obtaining a group and to save it in case of a need for transfusion. Clotting factor VIII was requested through the haematology laboratory.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "His chest X-ray was reviewed on the ward round. That was at 10.05 am..."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, for reference that's tile 186:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... and it was noted that there was some patchy consolidation at the right lower base, which could have suggested infection or aspiration (vomit or blood). At 13.45 hours later that day, I documented in the notes the results of the clotting screen as per the ward round."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's tile 225 if anyone wants to refer to it:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "These show continued low factor VIII levels and prolonged clotting time, which were very slightly better than those done on the day he was born. I do not recall any other involvement in [Baby N]’s care.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked with regards to the difficulty of intubation encountered with [Baby N]. All I can advise is, based on the notes and knowledge of the procedure, it is an inherently challenging procedure which is performed under pressure. Minor variation in anatomy from person to person will also affect the ease of this."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes Dr Henton's statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS BERNADETTE BUTTERWORTH (read)
The next statement, my Lord, please, at page 28 of the bundle, is from Bernadette Butterworth. She in a statement dated 14 May 2020 says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On the particular day in question, I had been working a long day shift on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Hospital. A long day starts at 07.30 and finishes at 20.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think I had been working in nursery 2. [Baby N] had been in nursery 1, being nursed in an incubator and being cared for by Lucy. I remember helping Lucy with the episode of desaturation and apnoea that [Baby N] is documented as having at 14.50 in Lucy's Meditech notes."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: For reference, that's tile 244 on the presentation:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I cannot remember exactly what my role was in helping Lucy or exactly how long I was assisting for. I can remember [Dr D] arriving and being present but cannot remember who else was present. I also cannot remember how I came to help Lucy. The unit is relatively small, so if Lucy had called for help or I had heard the monitor alarms going off, I would have gone to see if help was needed. In situations like this, anyone who is available would go and see if help was needed.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With regards to the intubation drugs that I had given to [Baby N] I can confirm that it is my signature against the morphine being given at 15.18, atropine being given at 15.21, and the suxamethonium also given at 15.23."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, did I say 15.23 for the second one? So it's 15.18, 15.23, 15.23:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I cannot remember if I physically administered the intubation drugs or if I just checked and countersigned for them.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In relation to the question asking if I remember the other episodes of desaturations and apnoeas that occurred at 07.15 and 19.40, I cannot. I would not have been on shift at 07.15 and the night shift commences at 19.30, so I would have been handing over at this time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do remember the ENT team from Alder Hey Children's Hospital had arrived and were present when I was leaving the unit that evening. I cannot remember any other involvement that I may have had with [Baby N] during this shift."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR ANTHONY UKOH (read)
My Lord, if I can go next, please, to page 55 of the additional statements in my Lord's bundle, it's Dr Anthony Ukoh. He says in a statement dated 6 November 2018:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked about my involvement in the treatment of [Baby N] and, in particular, the day shift of Wednesday, 15 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have had the opportunity to review the medical notes to assist with the preparation of this statement and I can confirm that I was working as a locum registrar within the paediatric department of the Countess of Chester Hospital on this day."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Pausing there, they've already been referred to and Dr Ukoh's notes appear at tile 178:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] was born slightly early. His mother was a haemophilia carrier. Following blood tests, it had been confirmed that he had inherited the haemophilia condition.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I examined [Baby N] at 09.45 hours on Wednesday, 15 June 2016 as part of a routine ward round. I had noted from the handover that [Baby N] had deteriorated overnight, become mottled and was suffering episodes of stopping breathing. There was a suggestion that he might have sepsis. There had been some oral bleeding.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] had been commenced on intravenous antibiotics and some breathing support in the form of BiPAP. When I examined [Baby N], I was made aware that he was still suffering from episodes of desaturation and bradycardia and was not stable.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] was unsettled at times and at times I noted his back to be arching. He was mottled in appearance and he had dried blood on his lips and in the oral cavity. I discussed [Baby N] urgently with Dr Caswell, paediatric haematologist consultant at Alder Hey Children's Hospital, who had advised commencing [Baby N] on the blood clotting protein factor VIII.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I also contacted the haemophilia liaison nurse in relation to obtaining the medication for its administration. I had no further involvement with the treatment of [Baby N] on this particular shift."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR SATYANARAYANA SALADI (read)
My Lord, next, please, Dr Saladi at page 30.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Saladi says in a statement dated 22 May 2019:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was the paediatrician of the week covering the wards from 8.30 to 4.30 pm every day from Monday, 13 June to Friday, 17 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was doing neonatal ward rounds on Wednesday, 15 June, after the handover from the night team at around 9 am.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On reviewing the notes, it was clear that [Baby N] had developed desaturations the previous night (14 June going into
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: the morning of 15 June) and he was transferred to nursery 1 for closer observation. It was noted that intubation was attempted three times but was not successful. [Baby N] was given support with BiPAP, a form of breathing support through [Baby N]’s nose, while he was breathing on his own.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After those events on the night of the 14th into 15 June, I saw [Baby N] on my ward round on the morning of 15 June 2016. The following clinical notes entry was made during the ward round by the junior doctor working with me that day. The notes record that [Baby N] was also seen by the day registrar prior to me reviewing his care on the ward round and the junior doctor working with me has recorded the following entry."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, in his statement Dr Saladi simply recreates what's on the notes. I wonder whether it would be easier simply to go to the notes in these circumstances.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Tile 167, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If it assists, I can read the script:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Ward round Saladi. Transfer to nursery 1. Profound desaturations to 48%. Attempted intubations x3. Blood in oropharynx, source unclear. Screened, on BiPAP, IV cefotaxime. Discussed with Dr Caswell this AM. For factor VIII, BD, 50 units per kilogram.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "V [for ventilation] BiPAP. F [feeding] IV glucose 10%, 2.6ml per hour, 150ml/kilogram/day. M [for medication]: intravenous cefotaxime. On examination: RR [which I think is respiratory rate] 28, PR 149."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Whether that's pulse rate I'm not sure but that would seem consistent:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "SaO2 [oxygen saturation]: 100%. Blood pressure: 88/51. Capillary refill time less than 2 seconds. Heart sounds 1 plus 2 plus 0. No abnormal posturing. Abdomen soft and non-tender.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Plan: (1) Group and save. (2) Factor VIII as per haematology. (3) Repeat CRP in 24 hours. (4) Parents updated. (5) Cranial ultrasound scan."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The entry records, returning to his statement:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The history obtained from the notes of the previous desaturations during the night which had been significant as his oxygen saturations had fallen to only 48% [as read].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Three attempts at intubation were unsuccessful and blood was seen in the oropharynx, which is the part of the throat at the back of the mouth. The source of the blood was unclear. A screen for infection was being undertaken. [Baby N] was receiving ventilatory support, that being BiPAP. He was also receiving intravenous antibiotics. [Baby N] had been discussed with the consultant haematologist, Dr Caswell at Alder Hey Hospital, by the paediatric registrar Dr Ukoh, who recorded that Dr Caswell advised factor VIII, a blood clotting protein, to be given.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I would have examined [Baby N] and the junior doctor working with me recorded [Baby N]’s respiratory rate, pulse rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, capillary refill time and his heart sounds. These findings indicated that [Baby N]’s condition was now stabilised. [Baby N] was not demonstrating abnormal posturing, which might have indicated a brain injury.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On examination his abdomen was soft and non-tender, which indicated that his desaturations were not due to an abdominal cause. The plan I formulated was for a blood sample to be taken to identify his blood group and an antibody screen in order that arrangements could be made for a blood transfusion if necessary.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The second step was for factor VIII to be given as per the advice received from the haematologist. I asked for a repeat CRP to be undertaken in 24 hours to confirm whether an infection was present. [Baby N]’s parents were updated about the events overnight and the plan and I also requested a cranial ultrasound scan to be performed. A record of the images in the notes revealed no brain haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The records show that I subsequently made a retrospective entry timed at 16.30 hours in [Baby N]’s medical notes, having been called to see him. My note is incorrectly dated 2015. It should be 2016."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, the note is again reproduced in the statement. If we could look behind tile 247, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Having corrected the date on the left-hand side, it's timed at 16.30, and reads as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Desaturated this afternoon at 2.50 pm with blood in the oropharynx and blood in the nasogastric tube. Improved with bagging. Elective intubation planned, following pre-medication. Unsuccessful attempts with two registrars and two consultants. Vocal cords difficult to visualise. Laryngeal airway placed by Dr Brearey. Baby received 2x 10ml per kilogram fluid bolus. Anaesthetic support requested. (Anaesthetists) assessing the baby. Discussed with Dr Bill Yoxall, Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If no success, advised to discuss with North-west Transport Service team and liaise with paediatric ENT team at Alder Hey. Parents are in the room and have been kept regularly updated with the clinical course."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then, "Saladi (consultant)", endorsed below.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: He continues in his statement:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My entry confirms that [Baby N] had further desaturations at 2.50 pm that afternoon. Blood was recorded in the oropharynx and in the nasogastric tube. His saturations improved by hand ventilation with an Ambu bag. Once again there were difficulties in intubating [Baby N], which included an attempt by me as well as Dr Brearey, another consultant colleague, who came to help.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Due to this, anaesthetic colleagues were called to provide specialist support. I discussed [Baby N] by telephone with the consultant neonatologist colleague [that's Dr Yoxall at Liverpool Women's Hospital] about difficulty in securing the airway. He advised seeking help from the North-west Transport Service along with the ENT team at Alder Hey for managing the difficult airway. [Baby N]’s parents were present and I kept them updated.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I made a further entry in [Baby N]’s records at 18.00 hours on the same day, recording the telephone call I had with Dr Frank Potter from Alder Hey, who was the paediatric intensive care consultant, and my entry read as follows."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think we need to go to this one, it's simply in text:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "15 June 16, 18.00 hours. Received phone call from Dr Frank Potter (Alder Hey PICU consultant) [that's the paediatric intensive care unit]. He will come with Alder Hey ENT consultant Ms Sue Day with a flexible bronchoscope. They will transfer the baby to Alder Hey with the NWTS ambulance, which will join them later. He asked for an Olympus light source suitable for an Olympus flexible bronchoscope. If baby is settled, no need to paralyse. Otherwise, give rocuronium."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the treatment options are listed as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "(1) Transfer to Alder Hey Children's Hospital with laryngeal mask airway. (2) Attempt intubation with flexible bronchoscope. (3) Tracheostomy if worsening airway.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have informed mother about the treatment plan. Dr Gibbs, the on-call consultant, is aware."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And again it is signed:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Saladi (consultant)."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: He concludes this statement, my Lord, with:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr John Gibbs was the consultant on call that evening from 4.30. I had handed over continuing care of [Baby N] to him. I had no further involvement in [Baby N]’s care on 15 June 2016 after my last entry. According to the notes, [Baby N] was subsequently intubated by Dr Frank Potter and he was transferred to Alder Hey Hospital intensive care unit during the night of 15 June 2016."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Second witness statement of DR SATYANARAYANA SALADI (read)
My Lord, there's a second statement from Dr Saladi at page 36 of the bundle, dated 23 January 2020, and in this he says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] has been seen in the paediatric unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital and by me on a regular basis since birth because he was born preterm at 34 weeks and because he has an inherited clotting disorder called haemophilia.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The reason [Baby N] is still seen by me is due to his haemophilia and, as we are the local hospital, if he has any injury or bleeding this will be the hospital he would come to.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He sees me for general paediatric medical problems and he sees a specialist at Alder Hey Hospital for the management of the haemophilia. [Baby N] is normally seen every 6 months. The last time I saw [Baby N] was on 19 November 2019. This was a routine review.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On examination, he looked well. He was pink, he was giving high fives, he had good eye contact and was playing imaginatively with teacups while I was talking to mum. With regards to the rest of the examination, including the functional neurological examination (which means that we observe them doing all of those things as they are playing to see if they have any weaknesses or are dragging one of their limbs whilst they are moving) is
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: appropriate [as read].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "There do not appear to be any headaches or any visual disturbances observed."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And under "examination" from that occasion it states:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] looked well today in clinic. Examination of his abdominal, cardiovascular and respiratory systems was unremarkable. His central line appeared healthy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I can see from [Baby N]’s medical records that prior to visiting Dr Whitby on 28 May 2019 [and these are the dates, my Lord as follows], 22 January 2018, 23 October 2018,25 April 2018, 26 March 2018, 24 October 2017, 27 March 2017, 3 October 2016, 18 August 2016, 1 July 2016."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's a total of nine appointments listed by Dr Saladi.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Over that period there were no major issues regarding his physical or cognitive development. Apart from the treatment for the haemophilia, which is the factor VIII, [Baby N] is not on any other medication and the only medical diagnosis is haemophilia and the preterm. We will continue to monitor [Baby N] for his growth and development.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With regards to the haemophilia, I am aware that during the neonatal period there were difficulties in putting the tubes into [Baby N] and he had a bleed when we were putting these in.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Any procedures can cause bleeding and the sort of procedures that little babies have, such as putting a feeding tube in from their nose to their tummy if they're too small to feed or, if they're having breathing difficulties, putting a tube into the windpipe, those are the procedures that can cause bleeding. I am aware that [Baby N] had bleeding from the oral cavity when he was receiving treatment on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "There was difficulty in putting the tube into the windpipe, so much so that the top part of the glottis (the voice box) was swollen and we could not put the tube in to support his breathing. We had to call an intensive care specialist from Alder Hey to come to the Countess of Chester Hospital and they came with an ENT surgeon to put the tube in so we could safely transfer [Baby N] to Alder Hey hospital. I have detailed this in my previous statement. Those are the sort of problems babies with haemophilia can develop if there is a lot of bleeding."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, that concludes that statement from Dr Saladi.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of [NURSE B] (read)
Next, please, page 43 in the bundle. It's a statement from [Nurse B]. She says in a statement dated 4 June 2020:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked with reference to my knowledge of [Baby N] and, in particular, the day shift of Wednesday, 15 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have had the opportunity to read his care notes to assist with this statement. I do remember baby [Baby N] for his diagnosis. I had never seen a neonate with haemophilia before. I was working a long day shift within the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember at the start of my shift being shocked to see [Baby N] poorly in nursery 1 as he had been almost ready for discharge home. I remember [Baby N]’s clinical condition deteriorating throughout this particular day and it ending in full resuscitation. I also remember that Nurse Lucy Letby was his designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] was situated in nursery number 1. If you were looking into nursery number 1 from the outside, he was in the space directly in front of the right-hand door.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do not remember having hands-on care with [Baby N]. However, I remember suggesting to Dr Brearey to use an I-Gel to secure [Baby N]’s airway when we were struggling to intubate him. I do not know why it was so difficult for the doctors to carry out this procedure.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I distinctly remember the desaturation that occurred at 19.50 hours so I must have been in nursery 1 at this time. The ENT doctors had gone with our consultant to look at labour ward theatre as this is where they were thinking of taking [Baby N] for intubation and possibly a tracheostomy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember seeing [Baby N]’s monitor showing a severe bradycardia, desaturation and seeing Nurse Lucy Letby responding to him. I do not remember who else was in the nursery at this time or who alerted the medical team to return and assist.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I can confirm that it is my initials against the blood gas readings taken at 15.11 and it is my signature against the administration of dexamethasone at 17.35 hours. I do not remember if this was for administering the drug or for countersigning. I remember that this drug was given at the request of the Alder Hey team to attempt to reduce any upper airway oedema that may have been there and to aid tracheal intubation."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS ELIZABETH MORGAN (read)
Next, my Lord, please, at page 45, a statement of Elizabeth Anne Morgan, dated 22 October 2021. She says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I, Elizabeth Morgan, have been asked to provide my professional opinion on the following question."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, we've had a statement from Elizabeth Morgan before, who is the expert nursing practitioner who's given an opinion in a previous case. As this is a subsequent statement, it doesn't contain her full description and qualifications, so just by way of reminder, if that's appropriate:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked to provide my professional opinion on the following question:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "'In interview, Lucy Letby said that she aspirated 1ml of fresh blood from the nasogastric tube but did not draw it to anyone's attention. How does this failure fit with good practice generally and in the case of a haemophiliac child in particular?'"

blocks.text: We've had a bit of an explanation from various witnesses along the way, but given this is your particular expert specialty, could you explain to the jury what haemophilia is, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Haemophilia is a bleeding disorder and it is quite a rare condition. It's one of the commonest -- it's top of the list, really, for difficulties, so people have often heard about it. Haemophilia is due to a reduction in a coagulation factor called factor VIII.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: The coagulation system is there to prevent us from bleeding catastrophically following injury and there is a step wide cascade of factors which activate following contact with broken blood vessels that activate one protein, that then activates another, so you get what's called a clotting cascade to eventually end up by making a blood clot that fills the hole in a blood vessel so that the bleeding stops.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Factor VIII is part of that cascade and so individuals who have no factor VIII, or very low levels of factor VIII, are at risk of bleeding, which can be catastrophic bleeding.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Would you like me to continue?
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes, please. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When we look at how severe haemophilia is -- factor VIII deficiency is called haemophilia -- we look at it in a range of nought to 100%. So 100% is within the normal range. Those with severe haemophilia have less than 1% levels of factor VIII in their bloodstream. People with levels of 1% to 5% have moderate haemophilia. Those with a factor VIII level of more than 5% and up to 40%, have mild haemophilia and everyone else is counted as being normal as far as haemophilia is concerned.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So people with factor VIII levels above 40% are in the normal range. So it's very tiny minority that is less than 1%, who are severe. And in this particular case, [Baby N] fell in the range of moderate haemophilia.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Just looking at what you've just explained to us in pure percentage terms, if I took an exam and got between 1% and 5%, I wouldn't describe that as a moderate result.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So can you just put the moderate of 1% to 5% in everyday terms and explain why that is moderate?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Looking at the percentage and looking then at the effect in individual people, individuals with factor VIII levels of less than 1% will have very major bleeding, so they're likely to have spontaneous bleeding. These are individuals -- and they are mostly men or boys, and I'll come on to that later. These will be people where even walking and having pressure on the knee joints can cause bleeding into their joints.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So it's very common to have joint bleeding. It's common to have mouth bleeding and it's very common to have much more excessive bleeding than you'd expect to see following a minor injury. So this might be bruises.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And a particular time to identify haemophilia is in children when they have intramuscular injections or vitamin K following birth because that can cause major bleeding into the muscle at the site of the injection.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Can I just stop you there, please? We've heard that in [Baby N]’s case, the administration of vitamin K was
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: deliberately not intramuscular. Would that be the explanation for why that decision was taken?

blocks.text: In [Baby N]’s case that is the reason for intravenous vitamin K not being given because there is a potential of him being haemophiliac because his mother is a carrier.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Would that decision have been taken also because vitamin K, habitually, is given very early, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's usually given on the same day of birth.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And by that stage, would it be the position that the precise position of the severity of [Baby N]’s haemophilia wouldn't have been established by that stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, it wouldn't, no. It takes some time.

blocks.text: So making sure that the position does no harm, first of all?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So that would be put off, all right. I'm sorry to have interrupted you. Would you carry on, please?

blocks.text: Individuals who have moderate haemophilia will have bleeds into the joints, into the muscles, or following dental surgery, et cetera, on a less frequent basis, but they would know what symptoms or their parents would know what symptoms to look out for with bleeding and bruising. blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: People with factor VIII levels more than 5%, who have mild haemophilia, will be covered with special administration of factor VIII, for instance if they were going to have surgery, to make a planned arrangement so that they wouldn't bleed catastrophically because we know that they have low factor VIII.

blocks.text: Now, I think you said a few minutes ago that boys are classically the people who manifest this particular condition. But perhaps you can explain why that is and also, if you would, the jury has heard that [Baby N]’s mother had a predisposition to this particular issue.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Haemophilia is an X-linked genetic disorder. So just to explain that, all of us have 46 chromosomes in our cells and in the nucleus of our cells. The chromosomes are parts of the genetic material which gives us the attributes that we have. It may be the colour of our eyes, our hair, how tall we are, et cetera.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: The chromosomes are paired, so there are two chromosomes 1, 2, et cetera. But the final pair, which are called the sex chromosomes, are different between males and females. So the female sex chromosome is the X chromosome and the male is the Y chromosome.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: If you look at the genetic material in these particular chromosomes, the female, the X chromosome, is much bigger than the Y chromosome. What that means, so far as biology is concerned, is there isn't a pair that then can allow for an abnormality on the missing part of what would be the extra part of the X chromosome. So if you have -- of the Y chromosome.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: If you have two X chromosomes, you are female. If you have an X and a Y you are male. So if a woman is a carrier for haemophilia, that would mean that she has an abnormality on one of the X chromosomes. It is countered by the normal X chromosome, so that female individual is likely to have a lower amount of factor VIII, but usually in the normal range or at the top end of the moderate range or mild range.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Can I check that I have understood that? So every female has two X chromosomes, no Y chromosome?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Every male has one X chromosome and one Y chromosome?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: The genetic issue that causes haemophilia always occurs on the X chromosome?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And females have two X chromosomes, therefore if there is an issue, a haemophilia issue, on one of the X chromosomes, in all likelihood the other X chromosome makes up for the deficiency --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: -- in the X chromosome that has the issue?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: To some extent?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, to some extent.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Sufficient to take you to within the normal range?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So although your particular reading between 1 and 100 may be low, it is still sufficiently low to get you within the normal range?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, usually.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And from a practical point of view, therefore, females who have the haemophilia gene or the haemophilia abnormality to the gene don't suffer the day-to-day issues that males do because they don't have the compensation in the other X chromosome?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Exactly. That's right.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: I think I understand. I hope I do. All right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's the background, if you like, the biological background to this particular issue?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: As a result of that, genetically speaking, what is the probability of a male child inheriting haemophilia?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's 50%. So it depends which of the maternal X chromosomes combine with the Y chromosomes from the father. So if it is the haemophilia-bearing X chromosome then that boy will have haemophilia.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If it's the other, then that won't be the case.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So putting it in more day-to-day language, if your mother has the genetic predisposition, you as a male child have a 50% chance of inheriting it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And you will have a problem to some degree because you don't have a compensatory extra X chromosome because you are a boy?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: As a result of that, in cases where the medical profession have identified that a particular mother has this genetic predisposition, is it an important thing for the gynaecologists to do to determine the sex of the child whilst or before birth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it's very important actually. So if a woman is known to be a carrier of haemophilia, it is very important that there is an attempt to be made to determine the sex of the
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: unborn child in order that birth can be managed sensibly to avoid issues for the child. Birth is quite a difficult process for people and therefore usually a caesarean section would be suggested.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes. Whilst there may be a whole range of reasons why a C-section is adopted in these cases, is the principal reason to prevent the likelihood of bleeds in the brain during a normal vaginal birth?

blocks.text: Yes, that is absolutely the case, and one of the things that I didn't say is that the most important types of bleeding are intracranial bleeding and neck and throat bleeding and gastric bleeding or gastrointestinal system bleeding in people with severe haemophilia.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes. The medical profession operates, at this stage of a child's entry to the world, on the basis that the child may have the most severe type of haemophilia?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, one has to be in that position, yes.

blocks.text: Exactly.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

What I mean is that an individual who's having an investigation to measure factor VIII, because there are certain situations where factor VIII may actually go up in cases of stress, et cetera, so the initial -- the first blood investigation to identify the amount of factor VIII is obviously important, but it's also quite important to keep an eye on that to make sure that that wasn't an elevated level because there may have been some activation or activity, eg infection, which I
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Dealing with the 15 June events, which we've been looking at here and what you're focused on, as the prosecution have explained to us, there's an issue, a factual issue, about the order in which intubation and bleeding takes place --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: -- and you've been asked about that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: You've explained that intubation, as with any instrumentation, may carry a risk of causing bleeding.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: May. It depends on the circumstances. Is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And if there's a baby with lower than normal factor VIII levels, with haemophilia, in the way, for instance, that [Baby N] had, does that increase the risk of bleeding from trauma?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... Not necessarily, no.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: If there is trauma, does that mean that bleeding is more likely?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If there is trauma?
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes, if there is trauma.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, if there is trauma then it is more likely.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And what you have said already about haemophilia leading to bleeding that would then be potentially more profuse would also apply?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it would.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And profuse, meaning more of it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, more of it, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Slower to clot?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, not clotting is the problem here with haemophilia, so the clots are very fragile and break down immediately, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you, Professor Kinsey. Those are the questions I've got.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR JOHNSON

Could I just clarify what we should take away from the last few questions and answers? You were asked whether haemophilia increased the risk of bleeding from trauma and you said not necessarily. And then you appeared to give an answer which could be interpreted as saying the opposite to that and it's probably a deficiency in understanding on my part rather than on your part in the way you expressed yourself. But can I give you an opportunity to clarify that? Somebody who suffers from haemophilia, are they more likely to bleed or is it that when they start to bleed, they don't clot?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It is in fact both. So individuals who have severe haemophilia can have spontaneous bleeding.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Let's leave people with severe problems out of it and focus, if we may, if only for my own benefit so that I don't get confused, on people who fall into [Baby N]’s category.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So somebody in [Baby N]’s category, who is immobile at his age, is he more likely to bleed than the child in the next cot of the same gestation who has a normal factor VIII level in their blood?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In a steady state situation, no -- well, he is at greater risk, but not from spontaneous bleeding.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes. So he won't just bleed for no reason?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, he won't just bleed for no reason. This is why I said earlier -- what I said is that individuals who are in the mild or moderate -- sorry, I mean moderate -- group is that they are not given factor VIII on a regular basis because it is not required.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes. Are you saying that it takes less trauma to induce, to start bleeding in somebody with [Baby N]’s
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: characteristics as compared to a child with factor VIII within the normal range?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I mean, the other way round. You need more trauma in an individual with normal factor VIII levels to induce bleeding or a collection of bleeding, bruising under the membranes. You might not necessarily see blood outside but you might see swelling.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So does it follow that, just picking up on your distinction between bleeding and bruising, bruising in effect is bleeding under the skin, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, bruising wherever it happens is contained -- well, it can be contained within an area where it isn't going to -- it can then have pressure around it, which would reduce the bleeding because of pressure in the area closing the hole. Does that answer your question?
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: I think in simple terms, blood comes from a vessel?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Indeed, yes. It does.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So in other words, it can be an artery, a vein, which is a big carrier of blood, or it can be a little capillary vessel from which one can bleed?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: If you bang your thumb with a hammer you can bruise it and that's subcutaneous bruising, bleeding under the skin you get?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Are you saying that someone of [Baby N]’s category, in terms of haemophilia, if he is subjected to a trauma, that his vessels are such that he is more likely to bleed than a child otherwise of his characteristics without haemophilia?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: He is more likely to bleed.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And that if he does bleed, his bleeding -- the blood will be slower -- will not clot?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The blood will not clot.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: You corrected me before. Will not clot.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Therefore there will be more blood, it'll either be subcutaneous under the skin or, if the trauma causes a rupture of the skin --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Then you'd get bleeding out of it.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: But there has to be a rupture of the skin?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Indeed, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Just picking up on that final point, somebody suffering with haemophilia, like [Baby N], does it take any more to rupture their skin than it would take to rupture the skin of a child who fell within the normal range?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Um... Technically, no, because the skin's integrity is the same. It's not a skin issue. But if the skin becomes stretched because there's bleeding underneath it or a bruise underneath it, then that will be more likely to burst open.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So the pressure of the bleeding would overcome the strength of the surface of the skin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes. Does your Lordship have any further questions.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, thank you, I think I've asked enough.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mr Myers, are there any questions you want to ask arising out of my questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, I'm grateful. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much for coming back and giving your evidence in relation to the issues that you have today. I assume not required again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't think so.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Are you aware of your being required again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, I haven't been.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: I'm told you won't be required again, so thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
Dr Evans, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: DR DEWI EVANS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Welcome back, Dr Evans. For the record would you identify yourself, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Dewi Evans.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. I hope I'm correct in saying that you have completed five separate reports or statements on the case of [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. They are dated, for the record, 3 June 2018?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: 17 January 2019?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then there is a pair on 21 October 2021?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As before, your initial statement was a sift?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The second statement was more considered?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And then subsequently, you've dealt with administrative issues such as pagination, but you've also given us some further detail on issues that have been raised with you after your considered report?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Just to put this case into the overall context, this was, I think, the 29th case that you were asked to look at?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. I would like to take, if we may, as a template for your evidence the report of 17 January 2019. There did you set out the circumstances surrounding [Baby N]’s birth —
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- which we have heard in evidence?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as the material that you were given, did that consist of the medical records from the Countess of Chester, which included some radiology material?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: An index and also some medical records from Alder Hey Hospital --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- in Liverpool?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Taking up, if we may, your report at paragraph 4 -- I'm looking at your overview to start with -- did you note the breathing issues, the grunting issues, that had occurred shortly after [Baby N] was born?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. These lasted for a few hours, soon after his birth, but settled quickly.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you also note the results of the blood tests, the coagulation results in particular?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did and noted that the factor VIII value was recorded at 3%.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Did you, as a matter of fact, towards the end of your report, invite the police to consult somebody with the sort of specialist knowledge that Professor Kinsey has?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you go on to consider the circumstances surrounding [Baby N]’s collapse at shortly after 01.00 hours in the early hours of 3 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And in particular, did you refer to the note made at the time by the doctor concerned, saying that [Baby N] had desaturated down to 40%?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: He was unsettled, there was an increased work of breathing?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: He looked mottled?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And dusky?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And screaming.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And screaming, of course, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You referred also, I think, to the nursing note entry made by Nurse Booth, which recounted the fact that [Baby N] had continued to cry, as it was put in the nursing note, for 30 minutes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thereafter, did you review the medical records covering the time following that and the events in the early hours of the morning of 15 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. What I found was that having recovered from this event on 3 June, his progress was pretty uneventful really. He was making satisfactory progress as you would expect of a baby who was premature but otherwise well.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you refer at your paragraph 13 to the events at 01.45 on the morning of 15 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: For anybody's note, they're at tile 80 and are [Dr A]'s notes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. I heard [Dr A]'s testimony yesterday and the note that he was -- had noticed mottling, which is a discolouration of the skin, and this -- but otherwise his heart rate and his heart sounds were normal, he had good air entry in
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: his lungs and his abdomen was normal and there were normal bowel sounds. They also did -- [Dr A] carried out blood gases, capillary gases.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They were all satisfactory. The lactate value was 3.2, which is minimally raised, but in isolation is not of clinical significance.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. And that in effect is what he told us yesterday?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you move on to consider [Dr A]'s notes which were at tile 84 in the second [Baby N] sequence and some desaturations which had been noted on the monitor?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Again -- we're talking about 05.15 hours?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, some more blood tests. So first of all, the capillary refill time was 3 seconds, and you'd want it to be 2 seconds or less really, so it's slightly increased and could be indicative of baby becoming unwell for some reason. His white cell count was 7.4, which is normal, in other words there was no indication of infection from the white cell count value. Platelet count 309, which is normal again. CRP value was less than 1, which again is a marker of infection, and a value of less than 1 is normal. But [Dr A] was sufficiently concerned, I think because the capillary refill time was slightly prolonged, to stop oral feeds and give a bolus intravenous infusion of 10% sodium chloride, which is standard practice, and he also added an antibiotic.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Again, we heard, I think, from [Dr A] about that yesterday.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you move on then to consider the notes that had been made by [Dr A] at 08.00 hours that same morning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did. These notes indicated a far more significant deterioration in [Baby N]’s condition because his oxygen saturation had dropped to 48%. Now, that is low and lifethreatening. His heart rate was 80. That is very low and very, very concerning. And those values were sufficient for him to require what he called bagging or being bagged up. He also had a mottled appearance of the skin once more and also reduced tone — in other words, he was more floppy.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So these are very concerning matters and were sufficient for him to be transferred to the intensive care nursery.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. You recorded additionally, I believe, the fact that [Baby N] had been given medication in preparation for an elective intubation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. He received morphine, which is a drug given for pain relief and for -- yes, pain relief. He also was given suxamethonium, which is a muscle relaxant, which one gives as a pre-med in anaesthetics to relax the muscles if you're preparing intubation. And he had atropine as well. So anyway, there were three efforts made. They were, sadly, unsuccessful.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. The jury has heard evidence yesterday concerning blood being seen at this stage of the process and no doubt the jury will come to their own conclusions in due course. But you have noted that fact, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, and it's clear from the evidence I've heard yesterday and from the notes I'd seen before that the blood was noticed in the oropharynx, in other words at the back of the throat, and the blood was present prior to the efforts at intubation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That, as you will understand, Dr Evans, I think is disputed on behalf of the defence.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay, right. That was my understanding anyway.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. That's one of the issues that the jury will in due course be invited to determine.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you go on to consider [Dr A]'s notes of [Baby N]’s vital signs together with those noted by Dr Ukoh at 10 am that morning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The 10 am notes noted a respiratory rate of 28, which is normal, a heart rate 149, normal, and oxygen saturation 100%, which again is clearly satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: His blood pressure was 88/51, which is absolutely fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And on this occasion his capillary refill time was less than 2 seconds, which is normal. In other words, showing normal perfusion of the skin. And again there was an additional note about there was no evidence of what they describe as abnormal posturing, in other words his tone was not abnormal. So these were normal findings.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you go on to note a later desaturation at or about 14.50 hours that afternoon?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did. Again -- which part is this?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We're at paragraph 19 of your report.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. He desaturated once more at 2.50 in the afternoon and the entry notes blood in the oesophagus and in the nasogastric tube and he required some resuscitation, he required bagging and, again, needed or was given two fluid boluses of sodium chloride, which is standard treatment in a situation of this nature.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We then heard evidence which you have summarised concerning a continuing series of events, which culminated ultimately at about 19.40 that same day when preparations were being made by the Alder Hey team to intubate [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Very striking that a number of people were unable to intubate [Baby N] during this afternoon, which is why they called the Alder Hey folk, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And we heard that [Baby N] required, after his collapse at that stage, CPR?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And received multiple doses of adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And sodium bicarbonate?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Six doses of adrenaline in all and sodium bicarbonate, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As part of your review did you look at the observation charts, in other words the yellow and white charts which the jury have hard copies of?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you also review the nursing entries, both from 3 June and 15 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did. Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So just going to page 20 of 27, please, Dr Evans. It's your observations section, paragraph 58. What overall view, in a
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: nutshell, did you take of [Baby N]’s progress from his birth until his collapse shortly after 01.00 hours on 3 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: My overall observation was that it was known that his mother was a carrier for haemophilia, but that he was well following his emergency caesarean section, not requiring much in the way of resuscitation. So therefore, that would have been satisfactory for a baby who's 34 weeks of age, gestational age.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you regard his deterioration at 01.00 hours on 3 June as being an everyday type of occurrence for a child in his position?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. In my sift report I overlooked it, let's be frank about that, but it was rather unusual in that he seemed to be fine at about 9 hours of age, and what was striking was this very sudden and very significant drop in oxygen saturation to 40%, so very low. He responded with 100% oxygen. We heard from the doctor who said she was crash called to something else, to another patient, sorry, and when she came back he was asleep, in air, with normal saturations. Therefore this very sudden onset of something with a very quick improvement, which is something very unusual.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Now, this apparent desaturation was associated with what Dr Loughnane described as screaming.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you think that was significant, the use of that particular word?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, it's very unusual for babies to cry other than when you're doing blood tests or causing some sort of discomfort, usually by putting intravenous lines in or taking blood tests from a heel prick. So they will cry.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But once you stop the procedure, they usually stop crying fairly quickly. They don't carry on crying.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As for screaming, this is an incredibly unusual description in my experience of a baby, 6 weeks premature, screaming. That's very unusual. And again continuing to cry for half an hour. So that was something that, having looked back on these notes, struck me as very unusual.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did the length of time, the 30 minutes -- is that -- it may be implicit from what you've already said, but is that unusual?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, the length of time is very unusual -- well, the fact of screaming, that the term screaming was used, is very, very unusual for a doctor to describe a baby in a baby unit, and the fact that it was the nurse, actually, who recorded the crying continuing for 30 minutes. So that is an exceptionally unusual finding in a neonatal unit and it's not what you would get because a baby is hungry, for instance.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So did you come to a conclusion as to what, in your view, had caused [Baby N] to react in that unusual way?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: By this time, of course, this is case 29, and I was aware of, you know, all the other cases we'd done because these files arrived with me later than the others, the first 28. It struck me that this baby might -- that something had been done to this baby to cause this episode of screaming. And so I went back over my notes, I went back over the overarching view I made in relation to injection of air into the circulation from other scientific papers, and there were a couple of them, a couple of papers, who described babies who had accidentally received an intravenous injection of air into the bloodstream and screamed, collapsed and died.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, all of that -- none of this was known to me before I became involved with this investigation, and of course it repeated what we've heard in previous cases with [Baby I], [Baby I], case 8, possibly [Baby E], where one heard, I think with [Baby E], this horrendous cry, as his mother described it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: [Baby I], again, a significant cry.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We know that babies who get intravenous air for whatever reason, there is an increased risk, hardly (inaudible) because they're small, of course, so you don't need as much air to cause problems. And secondly, they still have this hole in the heart, this foramen ovale, so any air can get from the right side of the heart into the left side of the heart. If it gets into the left side of the heart, it could get into a heart blood vessel, coronary artery. So technically, it could cause a heart attack, you know, which is incredibly painful. I can't prove any of this by the way.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's stick to, if we may, rather than getting involved more arcane areas, whether you thought that this particular event was a naturally occurring event, in other words whether it was one of the vagaries in behaviour of an infant on a neonatal unit or whether there was some other cause for it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This was unusual. This was unusual. This baby, very quickly following his birth, had recovered. So he was well at 9 hours of age. In other words, there was no grunting, one did not
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: have any of the features you get with breathing difficulties. So there was none of this and then suddenly, out of the blue, he collapsed very, very precipitously and this is what is remarkable.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Equally remarkable is the fact that he recovered so quickly. So for instance, if he had deteriorated because he was sickening for an infection, we're talking 3 June now, I would not have expected him to be back asleep, breathing in air, you know, soon afterwards. So therefore all of this, as we've heard several times, is incredibly unusual and not the sort of thing one has seen, despite one having spent most of one's career looking after babies in baby units.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So far as the issues of 15 June are concerned, the events of the early hours -- and by the early hours I'm talking about from midnight through to before 07.00 hours, okay?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In that period of time, did you draw any conclusions from the evidence as it was presented to you on paper and as you have heard it during this trial?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As I've heard it during this trial, and clearly it's much easier to form an opinion having heard everyone else's evidence, I would say that during the early hours his condition is what could be explained -- could be explained -- on the basis he was sickening for an infection. In other words, he was not quite as well, skin mottling, you know, that kind of thing, but not -- in other words, if I'd been there I would have done what [Dr A] had done and considered, "Hmm, he is sickening for an infection". We know the results subsequently did not prove an infection, but that is what I would have done. I would have done what [Dr A] did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You say the results didn't prove an infection thereafter, but looking at those results in the succeeding days, was there any evidence of an infection?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, none at all.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But thereafter, there are several collapses from 7.15 onwards. What view did you take of those events?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm not sure what -- it's quite difficult what to make of those. The key event for me was the fact that there was a deterioration around 8 am, which was more significant. In other words, his oxygen values dropped, his heart rate dropped significantly, and the most significant finding for me was that the doctors decided to intubate him, correctly, but when they
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: put a laryngoscope in to visualise the vocal cords, the back of the throat contained lots of blood --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- which meant that they were unable to intubate him, so they carried on with BiPAP.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So far as that is concerned, we've heard the factual evidence, we know where the issues lie between the prosecution and the defence. Would it be fair to say that your expert opinion can't really assist the jury in deciding whether the blood was there before the intubation or it was the intubation that caused the blood? It's a matter for them to look at the evidence and make their own minds up?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. If a doctor who had passed a laryngoscope said there was blood there, well, there was blood there.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
