blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That he was reviewed by the medics at 01.45?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We know what [Dr A]'s findings were. There was a
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: further examination at 03.45; is that right?
That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That examination was normal. The mottling that had previously been observed had resolved?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But there were some self-limiting desaturations recorded in the records?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The nursing records said that there were self-limiting desaturations, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. You record that a partial septic screen was performed and intravenous cefotaxime was given?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You then recorded a further medical entry at 05.15, which noted the persistence of mottling?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The prolongation to 3 to 4 seconds of the capillary refill time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the fact that a bolus of normal saline was given at that stage and [Baby N] was put nil by mouth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you then refer to Jennifer Jones-Key's nursing note at 07.15 concerning [Baby N]’s crying and dropping his saturations at 7.15 am?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the fact that he was seen by "Neonatal Nurse Lucy"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Following that, do you observe that after handover, [Baby N]’s saturations dropped again, he required bagging, and that care was handed over to "Nurse Lucy"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Next, do you record [Dr A]'s examination or review of [Baby N] after a profound desaturation to 48%?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That he was given medication in preparation for intubation at around 08.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And whether before or afterwards, before or after an attempt to intubate, blood was seen in the oropharynx?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thereafter, at 09.45, did you observe that the notes recorded dry blood in [Baby N]’s mouth and on his lips?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He remained mottled and he was having intermittent episodes of extensive posturing and arching?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Could you just translate that into language I can understand, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Usually, newborn babies like to be -- adopt a flexed posture. That's where your arms and legs are bent, and anyone
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: who's seen a newborn baby know they like to be scrunched up. If you have extensive posturing, your arms are straight and twisted out, that's a very abnormal movement, and your legs are pointing straight with your toes pointing downwards. So that's a very abnormal posture for a newborn baby to adopt.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You then record the advice from Alder Hey to give factor VIII?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The fact that that was administered at 11.00 hours and a clotting screen was performed at that time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There was a further desaturation at 14.50 down to 44%?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And fresh blood was noted in [Baby N]’s mouth and 3ml of blood was aspirated from the nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry then intervened. He saw what he has told the jury he saw in [Baby N]’s throat.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The anaesthetists were called, the local anaesthetists first of all, and then that was followed by the team from Alder Hey and the events of about 19.40 to 19.45 when [Baby N] was intubated by Dr Potter and the events happened that we heard of yesterday from a number of the medical practitioners?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This included, of course, several doses of adrenaline, an infusion of adrenaline, together with two doses of sodium bicarbonate?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can we move then to your observations and opinion, Dr Bohin. I'm looking now at your paragraph 7.1.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you summarise the position for us from [Baby N]’s birth through to the events of the early hours of the following day, 3 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, of course. [Baby N], as we know, was born early.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He was premature but only 5 weeks premature. And in keeping with that degree of prematurity he was a well baby. He developed some grunting after birth, so some respiratory distress after birth, and this continued for 4 hours. And therefore he was started on antibiotics after a septic screen. And that's completely standard practice in neonatal medicine.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The CRP at that time was less than 1 and his blood cultures were subsequently negative but nevertheless that was the right course of action to take. As part of that septic screen a chest X-ray was taken and that showed signs in both lungs of possible infection, but regardless of that, he settled down quite quickly and was soon in air and all his observations were normal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So whether he would have settled anyway or because of the antibiotics, we'll never know. But in any case he settled.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Just interrupting you for a second, so far as the chest X-ray is concerned, that has been seen by Professor Arthurs, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it has.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You know what he says. We are not going to advertise it now, but in due course you know that he will come and tell the jury about his views --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- as far as that is concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: But just staying within your expertise if we could, could we move on to the events of 01.00 or 01.15 on the morning of the 3rd, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At just over 11 hours of age, so at around 01.00 hours the 3rd, [Baby N] had a profound desaturation to 48%, which is a significant desaturation as we have heard.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This is a life-threatening desaturation. He was noted to be crying and the registrar said was screaming and that he apparently cried for 30 minutes, which is really very, very unusual for babies to cry for that length of time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's rare for preterm babies to cry for long periods. Of course they cry, all babies cry, but they don't cry for long periods unless they're in significant pain or discomfort because they very easily can be settled. We have to undertake quite uncomfortable and distressing procedures often on newborn babies
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: and some of those procedures are painful, so of course they do cry. But you can usually cuddle them or settle them with a dummy or contain them and they stop crying quite quickly.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In my experience they don't continue to cry for 30 minutes and nor would a neonatal nurse let them cry for 30 minutes without trying to comfort them in some way. I have never heard a neonate scream. Babies will cry, but I've never heard them scream. So on reviewing the notes, there was nothing to indicate that [Baby N] had undergone any sort of painful or unpleasant procedures immediately prior to that event to account for what was clearly a very prolonged episode of distress.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you, in the context of all that, come to any view as to the possible causes for why [Baby N] would have been demonstrating that type of behaviour?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, I could only conclude that this was secondary to an inflicted painful stimulus because something had caused him to be very unsettled, to desaturate with a life-threatening desaturation, and then cry and scream for that period of time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Once he had settled, everything reverted to normal, and that was extremely odd, and the only thing I could think of to account for that was an inflicted painful stimulus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you feel that you were able to go any further than saying that, an inflicted painful stimulus?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can we move on, please, to 15 June 2016. In your paragraph 7.5, did you record the fact that following that event in the early hours of 3 June, until almost exactly the same time on the 15th, [Baby N] had remained well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, he hadn't given any cause for concern to the clinical staff.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We have heard evidence over the last couple of working days that he began to have desaturations and became mottled at various stages at about 1 o'clock, some time after 3 am and some time after 5 am.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you see anything unusual in that sequence of events up to and including the events at about or just after 5 am that morning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, I mean, it was odd. We knew that in the past he had had lot of self-correcting desaturations, which would be normal for a baby of this age. But on these occasions there seemed to be mottling, which was coming and going, depending on -- [Dr A] saw it, then it seemed to have gone, then it came back again, so that was something that was present. That isn't diagnostic of anything, but it does alert you to the fact that something may not be well and you need to keep a watch on things to see if the baby may be developing any infection and to look at their observations to see if things are deteriorating. That was exactly what [Dr A] said.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And eventually, he decided that things were so not right that he changed the antibiotics to a different antibiotic. Then because of the continued desaturations, he decided he ought to intubate and ventilate [Baby N] because although he didn't quite know why this was happening, he felt that he needed respiratory support.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We know there was a marked desaturation at about 07.15 and that at or about 08.00 that morning when [Dr A], having medicated [Baby N] for intubation, decided to look into his mouth, he saw, either before or after he'd tried to intubate him -- and you will understand, I'm sure, that there is controversy about this as between the prosecution and the defence --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- he saw blood.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If the blood was there before the attempt to intubate, which is a matter the jury will have to decide, can you conceive of any natural cause for that having happened?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I looked -- well, firstly there was -- it was not possible to establish with certainty where that blood may be coming from. [Dr A] was the only person that looked down and he couldn't establish where that blood was coming from. But in any case, blood was in the oropharynx and I felt that there were three possibilities.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: One, there could be local bleeding within the mouth.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Secondly, there could be bleeding from the stomach or the gut, which had come up into the mouth. Or thirdly, there could be bleeding from below the vocal cords.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Those were the three things that I felt needed to be considered and either confirmed or excluded.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What views did you reach?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, the chest X-ray taken on the 15th was reported as being compatible with infection rather than pulmonary haemorrhage, but regardless, [Baby N] wasn't a baby that was likely to have pulmonary haemorrhage. We see it in babies who are much more premature and in older babies when they have been very unwell for a long time. And he didn't fit into that category. So he wasn't a baby that you would suspect to have a pulmonary haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Babies who do have pulmonary haemorrhage, it can be catastrophic. What you see when you try to intubate them is copious amounts of blood coming up from the vocal cords and when you suck it out it's replaced by more blood that you can see coming up from below the vocal cords and that wasn't something that [Dr A] described. He did say he was unable to view the tracheal inlet when suction was applied, but he didn't say he could see blood coming up from below the vocal cords.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And my other reason for thinking this was not a pulmonary haemorrhage was the swiftness of the recovery, because babies who have pulmonary haemorrhage need almost certainly ventilating and they need ventilating at very high pressures, whereas, as we know, [Baby N] wasn't intubated on that occasion, but was put on to BiPAP and was ventilated on BiPAP at very low pressures. So again, that doesn't fit with a pulmonary haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Bleeding locally from the mouth or stomach. If there'd been bleeding from the stomach we would have had repeated aspirates from the nasogastric tube thereafter, and that didn't happen. So I felt that actually, it couldn't have come from the stomach.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far you favour excluding pulmonary haemorrhage, from the lungs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Gastrointestinal --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- ie from the stomach, haemorrhage? So what --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We're left with local trauma to the mouth. At that stage, I can't confirm or refute local trauma to the mouth. All we had at that stage was [Dr A]'s account that he couldn't see a -- he didn't say he saw a bleeding point, all he saw was lots and lots of blood, so we can't say whether that was from the mouth at that stage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Would you agree with -- from your paediatric perspective, would you agree with Professor Kinsey, who told us that she would exclude spontaneous haemorrhage, in other words there has to be a cause?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, there needs to be some sort of trauma to the mucosa to then have a reaction which either causes a bruise or, if that bruise is sufficient, the skin gets breached and it then causes a haemorrhage. But in babies with haemophilia, as she said this morning, that degree of haemophilia, they don't just haemorrhage spontaneously.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Because of the existence of haemophilia in this case, and I'm looking at your paragraph 7.14, did you specifically say that a more haematologically specialised opinion should be sought to cover the possibilities?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, because in my professional career I have only looked at three babies with haemophilia. It is rare, but I have looked after three babies and therefore I am not an expert on haemophilia and she is. So I felt someone else should give an opinion on that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So summarising the position, Dr Bohin, could you deal first with the events of 3 June as to what your view was -- what the evidence drove you to conclude must have happened in the early hours of the 3rd?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: For me, my opinion was that the most likely cause of the event on the 3rd was inflicted trauma to the mouth or oropharynx.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the events of the 15th, and we have an ongoing situation from 7.15 through to almost exactly 12 hours later, actually, culminating in a fairly catastrophic collapse requiring the administration of adrenaline and other drugs, could you identify a natural cause for that series of events?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't identify a cause for the bleeding, a natural cause for the bleeding that caused [Dr A] to fail his attempted intubations in the early morning. But of course thereafter -well, I think there was some sort of inflicted trauma that caused the bleeding, and I know that's a matter of debate at the moment, but I think there was some inflicted trauma which led to bleeding, which caused [Dr A] not to be able to intubate. Thereafter, with successive people trying, it becomes much more difficult. As we heard yesterday from Dr Potter, the more people that try, there causes more swelling of the back of the throat, so the anatomy becomes very distorted, and so the more people that try, the more difficult it becomes. And we know from the other medical staff that tried to intubate that there appeared
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: to be a swelling at the back of the throat so we know that the anatomy was distorted.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think this culminated in the cardiac arrest because the airway then was just not sustained by the laryngeal mask because of the degree of swelling in the airway.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Bohin. Would you wait there for some further questions, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Bohin, following the same order and starting with 3 June, your conclusion is that what happened -- first of all is consistent with inflicted painful stimuli; is that correct.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: And can be explained by that, that's what you say?

blocks.text: I was picking up in fact on the question that there'd been a course that had run from 8 o'clock to 19.40 or thereabouts, I think you were asked by the prosecution, and I'm just establishing that in fact, if we go back, we can take this back from 01.45 right the way through, can't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you've touched on what happened as the day went on.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There is no specific site of trauma identified at any point, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's not. But I think, as Dr Potter said yesterday, when you're the person that's performing a life-saving manoeuvre, your prime objective is to, as I think he put it, put the tube in the hole. So what you don't do is spend a lot of time looking round the anatomy. If you can't achieve your objective by placing the tube in the right place then clearly you will write down why that is the case. But if you get the tube in, then you're not -- you don't have a good look around because the baby becomes unwell. Every time somebody tries the baby becomes more unwell. So if you have a look and you can't see the anatomy because it's obscured, the right thing to do is stop. So I think those that saw something odd wrote that they saw something odd but the fact that it isn't there, I don't think we can take much from that.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I disagree with Dr Potter on that, to be honest.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And I think, as she said in her read-out statement, that's not at all unusual for that to happen. But of course he was 9 kilos by then and he was only 1.67 kilos at this stage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR JOHNSON
Just one matter please, Dr Bohin. You said you disagreed with Dr Potter about that and I just wanted to clarify precisely what it was you disagreed with him and why.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Potter was asked whether the effect of dexamethasone that was given, I think, at about half past 5 -- um...
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'll get the time.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This was attributable to me, wasn't it, asking the question?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, that was a very good question. It was about the dexamethasone given about 2.5 hours before the intubation. We know from research where dexamethasone is given to older children with croup, so that's not like this case but it's in older children, that actually it works within about 2 hours. So this is children who are toddlers, usually, who come into the emergency department with life-threatening croup and that treatment is to give them, dexamethasone, and that works within about 2 hours. So I'm not suggesting that all the swelling had disappeared by 2 hours, but certainly we know that the onset occurs within 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And in -- and there is a Cochrane -- there's a big research base on that and, in addition to that, although [Baby N] was given adrenaline because of his profound bradycardia and his cardiac arrest, for want of a better word, adrenaline is also given for people who have major anaphylactic reactions and initially it's given intramuscularly, but if people have life-threatening airway problems in anaphylaxis, adrenaline is given intravenously and it's given every 5 minutes. So that must work almost immediately or it wouldn't be given that frequently. And it was on that basis that I disagreed with Dr Potter that the effects of dexamethasone 2.5 hours earlier may have reduced the swelling so may have made his attempt at intubation easier.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I have to say, he did use something called a bougie, which is a kind of a firm tube, a thin tube, that he used in order to intubate, and anaesthetists don't do that unless there's a problem with intubation. So it made me think that actually the intubation wasn't as straightforward as we were perhaps thinking it might have been.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can I break all that down a little bit, please. Can we start with, just so that we have this reference, please, tile 288 in the second sequence. Thank you. That shows us that the dexamethasone was given at 17.35. Of course these events in which Dr Potter was most directly involved happened at 19.40. You say that dexamethasone is prescribed for croup. Older -well, maybe not only old people remember croup. What is croup, first of all?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Croup is a viral infection of the throat, really, and it causes swelling of the throat, and children make a characteristic crowing sort of noise so you know that they've got some airway obstruction. They make a very characteristic noise and when they cough they bark like a seal and that shows you that the airway is narrowed in order to make that noise.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So why would -- it's all very straightforward to you because you know all this, but we don't. Why would dexamethasone be given as a treatment for croup?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because it's an anti-inflammatory, so it very quickly reduces swelling. So in young babies where they've got this swelling of the throat, it works very quickly to relieve that swelling so that you don't then have to go on to intubate them or give them respiratory support.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do anaesthetists deal with children suffering from croup?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Only if it's not worked and they need to intubate them as a matter of urgency.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Who deals with children suffering from croup?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Paediatricians and the emergency department and GPs.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you have experience of this?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have experience of croup and also giving dexamethasone to babies who -- neonates on a neonatal unit who have been intubated for a long time because if you are a very sick newborn baby and you need to be on a ventilator for a period of time, the physical presence of a tube in your trachea causes localised swelling, and so when babies are well and can be extubated and that tube is taken out, there's usually quite a lot of swelling around the vocal cords, which means that babies then don't manage with the endotracheal tube taken out, and so we tend to give dexamethasone prior to extubating those babies to reduce any swelling so that when you do remove the breathing tube, the babies remain well and you don't have to replace it. So I've experience of both of those things.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Now turning to adrenaline in this context, you've talked about anaphylaxis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which is an overreaction of the system to something that you're allergic to; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And a classic, dangerous -- so the nut type allergy, a real nut allergy?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So somebody who, if they have a particular nut, whether it's a peanut or a tree nut to which they are allergic, they can suffer an extreme allergic reaction?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. It comes on very quickly, starts off with hives, they get a feeling of swelling in their throat, because that's exactly what's happening, swelling of their airway, and a feeling that they can't breathe. They can't breathe because their airway is being blocked because that is the symptom of the anaphylaxis.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The treatment for that, the standard treatment, is an EpiPen, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: An EpiPen is something that is carried around or should be carried around by people who have a diagnosed --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Are you happy with -- you're just leading the witness.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm sorry.

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry. This is because you're not meant to lead your own witness. In other words, you shouldn't suggest the answer to your own witness. Cross-examining is very different. You suggest the answer and hope the witness will agree with your question.

blocks.text: People who have allergies, whether it be to peanut -- I think, you know, that's the commonest allergy certainly in the United Kingdom. Sufferers of severe peanut allergy carry an EpiPen, which is adrenaline in a little pen form, and if they are accidentally exposed to that allergen they know very quickly that they've been exposed to it and they use the EpiPen to give themselves an intramuscular injection, so they -- kind of usually in their leg or their tummy. They give themselves an injection and that EpiPen contains adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They then go to an emergency department as quickly as possible because the adrenaline wears off and you may need -- depending on the amount of exposure and your symptoms, you may need more than one dose of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But, of course, if you arrive at an emergency department they are in a position where they can put in an intravenous line and give you adrenaline intravenously, which works much more quickly than intramuscularly.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Intramuscularly is brilliant, but intravenous is much better.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In that context how quickly does adrenaline have to work to unblock the airway in order to have an effect?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, if you give it intravenously, it's immediate, but the effect is fairly short-lived, so you may have to give multiple doses of adrenaline and if then that doesn't work, you're left with having to put an airway into the patient and intubating them.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that the reason you respectfully -- or you disagree with Dr Potter and his assessment in relation to dexamethasone and adrenaline?
